title: World Cup co-hosts Mexico back Gianni Infantino despite Concacaf’s calls for ‘reckoning’
content:
The Mexican Football Federation (FMF) has pledged its support to Gianni Infantino despite the fallout from FIFA’s failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Concacaf, the confederation of North, Central America and the Caribbean, had called for a “comprehensive reckoning” on Infantino’s presidency.

The FMF was joined by the Argentine Football Association (AFA) in endorsing the FIFA president.

This followed UEFA doubling down on its threats to boycott the World Cup, having released a statement over the weekend announcing that it had lost confidence in Infantino’s leadership.

World Cup co-hosts Mexico, however, have backed the FIFA president. The FMF said in a statement that it “aligns itself with the call issued by President Infantino … to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of the 211 member associations.”

The statement concluded: “The FMF supports President Infantino’s leadership in continuing to drive the development of football through institutional strengthening.”

FIFA had planned to sell stakes in a new entity, called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), that it was planning to set up to run its major tournaments and events. World football’s governing body wanted to sell a fifth of FFE to an investor group led by Thrive Eternal — a U.S. investment fund run by Joshua Kushner, the brother of President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner — for $4.2billion (£3.1bn).

Conmebol, the governing body of South American football, admitted in a statement on Thursday its “concern” over the situation due to the lack of consultation, but emphasises the importance of “preserving the unity of the football family” ahead of March’s FIFA elections.

Conmebol member association the AFA acknowledged the “uncertainty” that the proposals had caused, but praised the “profound transformation” Infantino had brought to FIFA.

“On behalf of the Argentine Football Association (AFA), and its Executive Committee, we address you, dear President… to express our support for the management carried out during the last 10 years,” the statement began, before concluding that the best “way forward” was to continue working under Infantino’s leadership.

Mexico and Argentina joined other associations including Morocco, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates in supporting Infantino. A number of European associations, including England, Wales and Sweden, have withdrawn their backing.

President of the Norwegian federation (NFF) Lise Klaveness, a frequent critic of Infantino’s, has said her association would ask the FIFA president to resign, in an interview with the Guardian.

Infantino received “full support” from FIFA’s senior leadership in attendance at a crisis meeting in Morocco on Wednesday. He is standing for re-election at a congress in March.

The Confederation Africaine de Football (CAF), which represents African nations, released a statement on Thursday in which it “unanimously reconfirmed its support” for Infantino, and said it was committed to continuing to work together with the world governing body.
